# Contributing to Keyline

## Set up

Node.js 24 (`.nvmrc`) and pnpm, at the version pinned in `package.json` (`corepack enable` provides it). Then:

```sh
pnpm install
pnpm exec playwright install chrome chromium firefox webkit     # on Linux add --with-deps
```

`pnpm-workspace.yaml` holds two supply-chain settings. `minimumReleaseAge` keeps any package version published in
the last 24 hours out of an install, so a compromised release is usually found and pulled before it can reach
the repository; if you need a fix released today, wait a day rather than lowering it. `onlyBuiltDependencies`
lists the packages allowed to run install scripts (none at present); add one only when it fails without its
script, with the reason beside it.

## How the repository fits together

Keyline ships as a shadcn **registry**: a set of **items** (a component, a shared library, the theme) that the
shadcn CLI copies into someone else's project. Everything else in the repository exists to build, exercise or
document those items.

- **`src/registry/`** is the product. `src/registry/keyline/` holds the source (each component is
  `ui/<name>.tsx` with its `ui/<name>.css`). Each item has a `<name>.meta.ts` beside its source (typed by
  `src/registry/item.ts`): its title, description, files, CSS file and dependencies. `sidebar` and `alert-dialog`,
  which only install other items, live in `src/registry/keyline/virtual/`.
- **`site/public/r/`** is the built registry, one JSON file per item, which is what `npx shadcn add` downloads.
  The documentation site serves it at `/r/{name}.json`, so deploying the site publishes the registry. It is
  generated by `pnpm registry:build` (`scripts/registry/build.ts`, which also writes the index, `registry.json`)
  and committed. The build reads imports and `kl-` class names to work out each item's npm and registry
  dependencies and fails when they differ from what the meta declares; a dependency the source cannot show goes
  under the meta's `requires`, with its reason. It also fails when a file that needs `"use client";` lacks it
  (written with the semicolon; the build script says why). `pnpm registry:verify` then checks the built JSON on
  its own terms: every import is declared and every dependency is built.
- **The theme is generated.** Every token is data in `src/registry/keyline/theme/tokens.ts`; the shared CSS that
  derives colours and draws frames, rows and focus is `theme/foundation.css`. `pnpm registry:build` first runs
  `scripts/registry/theme.ts`, which writes `theme/keyline.css` and `theme/keyline-shadcn.css` from them. Edit
  those two sources, never the generated files; a unit test fails when they differ. `tests/theme/` installs the
  built theme through the shadcn CLI's own CSS updaters and fails if any rule or value is lost or moved.
- **`src/lib/utils.ts` and `components.json`** stand in for a consumer's shadcn setup. Components import `cn()`
  from `@/lib/utils`, as they will in an installed project (`@/` is `src/`).
- **`src/demo/`** is the demo app (`pnpm dev`). Its specimen page shows every component in its states, one
  **specimen** per component in `src/demo/specimens/`. The browser tests run against it.
- **`site/`** is the documentation site (`pnpm site:dev`): a page and examples per component, built with
  Keyline's own components.
- **`tests/`** holds unit tests (`tests/**/*.test.ts`), part tests (`tests/parts/`) and page specs
  (`tests/browser/`; its [README](../tests/browser/README.md) covers both), compile-only type tests
  (`tests/types/`) and consumer checks (`tests/consumer/`), which install items into fresh
  projects.
- **`docs/`** holds [usage.md](../docs/usage.md) for people installing Keyline, [design.md](../docs/design.md) for
  the design model every component follows, and [releasing.md](../docs/releasing.md) for publishing a version.

## Making a change

1. Edit the component in `src/registry/keyline/` and watch its specimen in `pnpm dev`.
2. Run the tests for what you touched: `pnpm test:parts <name>` runs its part tests and
   `pnpm exec playwright test <name>` every page spec whose file name matches, in every engine. Each run builds its own snapshot of the app, so edits made while it runs are not tested.
3. Look at it across modes when the change is visible. `pnpm capture -- <data-testid>` screenshots one element
   in light, dark, compact, RTL, narrow and reduced-motion configurations in both engines, and writes the images to
   `.artifacts/captures/`. The specs assert on geometry, styles and the accessibility tree rather than pixels, so
   this is how a visual change gets seen.
4. If the change affects what an item installs (its files, CSS, imports, or its meta), run
   `pnpm registry:build` and commit `site/public/r/` and `registry.json` with it. `pnpm test` and CI fail when
   they are out of date.
5. Run `pnpm lint` and `pnpm format` (which rewrites files in place) as you go.
6. Run `pnpm check` before opening a pull request. It takes about five minutes and runs, in order:
   - `pnpm typecheck`: the source, the tests (`tsconfig.tests.json`), the scripts (`tsconfig.scripts.json`) and
     the site, under the strict compiler options in `tsconfig.json`. Fix an error at its cause; a `!` or a cast
     carries a comment saying why it is safe.
   - `pnpm lint`: oxlint with type information, configured in `.oxlintrc.json`, with no warnings allowed. Keyline's
     own rules live in `lint/keyline-plugin.ts`; `keyline/no-radix-idioms` keeps Radix idioms and `dark:` utilities
     out of `src/registry/`. A rule is either an error or off, and turning one off needs the reason beside it.
   - `pnpm format:check`: oxfmt, configured in `.oxfmtrc.json`. Fix it with `pnpm format`.
   - `pnpm test`: unit tests, including the install commands in the docs, the built registry (that it equals a
     fresh build, and what every shipped item must and must not contain) and the lint guard.
   - `pnpm test:types`: compile-only type tests for the generic parts.
   - `pnpm registry:build`, `pnpm registry:verify`, every part test (`pnpm test:parts`), every page spec (`pnpm test:browser`) and the
     CSS-order check (`pnpm test:css-order`). Neither browser runner retries a failed test.

Two slower checks run when they apply:

- `pnpm test:consumer`, when a change affects installation. It installs items from a fresh registry build into
  new Vite + shadcn apps (all together, one at a time, and with the opt-in shadcn theme) and a Next.js App Router
  app (`src/`, a `~/*` alias, stock shadcn beside Keyline, repeated installs), then type-checks, builds and
  exercises them in Chrome and WebKit. It needs network access. CI runs it on every pull request.
- `pnpm test:site`, when a change affects the documentation site. Start the site first with
  `pnpm site:build && pnpm site:start`.

All test, capture and consumer output goes to `.artifacts/`, which is ignored.

## Adding a component

A new component is done when it has all of these:

- source in `src/registry/keyline/ui/`, following [docs/design.md](../docs/design.md)
- a `ui/<name>.meta.ts` beside it (copy a neighbour's), with `site/public/r/` rebuilt
- a specimen in `src/demo/specimens/`, wired into `src/demo/App.tsx`
- a page and example in `site/`
- a part test in `tests/parts/` running the conformance suite and axe over every exported part, with any failure it
  cannot fix yet recorded in `tests/parts/known-failures.ts`
- page specs in `tests/browser/` covering behaviour, keyboard, focus and the accessibility tree in every engine

## Rules, and why

- **Demos, the site and consumer tests use the public API.** Compose with props, Tailwind utilities and the `kl-`
  role utilities, and hook tests onto `data-testid`. Internal `.kl-*` classes can change at any time, and a
  consumer has nothing else to work with. When a composition seems to need an internal class, that is an API gap:
  fix the component, or record the gap.
- **Wrap the library shadcn uses** for the same job (react-resizable-panels, react-day-picker, recharts,
  embla-carousel), pinned to an exact version, and build everything else on Base UI primitives. Hand-written
  behaviour misses the edge cases those libraries already handle.
- **The documentation site is built from Keyline**: its shell, navigation, scroll areas and tables are Keyline
  components. That way the site keeps testing the library.
- **Fix the cause.** A failure that depends on sub-pixel position or timing gets its bias removed, the fix is
  checked across offsets, and the guard test is shown to fail on the old code.
- **A check stays as strict as it was.** Fix the code rather than loosen an assertion or a tolerance. A
  `test.skip` names the engine limitation that requires it.

## Pull requests

Keep each pull request to one change, and say what a reviewer should look at. Visible changes need before and
after captures.
